newsitem.title: USA: EchoStar Wars--analysts differ over firm's ratings.
newsitem.headline: EchoStar Wars--analysts differ over firm's ratings.

text.p: While it is not unusual for Wall Street professionals to quibble privately over debt ratings, a disagreement over the rating of junk bonds from EchoStar Communications Corp has recently turned into a public spat.

In a recent research report, Michael Weiner, high-yield media and telecommuncations analyst at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc, wrote that Standard & Poor's had incorrectly rated the debt of various holding companies of EchoStar Communications.
S&P contends its ratings are correct and says it has no plans to change them.
At issue is S&P's assignment of a B-minus rating to $375 million in new junk bonds sold in June by EchoStar DBS Corp, a new EchoStar holding company.

At the same time, S&P lowered the rating to CCC-plus from B-minus of $580 million in outstanding zero coupon bonds issued in 1996 from a seperate holding company called EchoStar Satellite Broadcasting Corp.
It also cut the rating to B-minus from B of $624 mllion in zero coupon bonds from EchoStar's operating company, Dish Ltd.
Weiner argues that S&P incorrectly rated the new bonds as senior to the 1996 bonds. In actuality, holders of the 1996 bonds are senior to the new bondholders in the capital structure, he said.

Robert Nelson, the S&P analyst on EchoStar, defended the ratings actions, saying the capital structure was not an important consideration. "The (credit) structure didn't enter into it at all because the indenture of the original (operating company) notes is so restrictive that the credit worthiness of (the operating) company and its cash flow had to rise dramatically before it becomes an issue," Nelson said.
Nelson said S&P placed more importance on the value of different satellites which secured the two bonds as well as the total debt issued by each holding company.
S&P changed its rating on the outstanding EchoStar issues because it felt that the company's business had deteriorated, he added.

Weiner said Moody's Investors Service Inc shared his views on the issue. Moody's rated both bonds Caa1 but acknowledged the seniority of the 1996 bonds by assigning them a positive outlook while assigning only a stable outlook to the new bonds.

"We were very conscious of the subordinatation issue. We took an unusual measure by differentiating the outlook on one piece of debt versus another (because of the subordination issue)," said Bob Konefal of Moody's.
